title: Accessible Garden Weeding Tool
short_description: An inclusive-design telescoping weeding tool for elderly and mobility-impaired gardeners, taken from market research through to a manufacturable design.
full_description: A team inclusive-design project (coursework code PD-77) to design a device enabling people with limited mobility and dexterity to remove garden weeds across different soil types without bending, kneeling, or high grip force — covering user research, concept generation, materials selection and a lifecycle/manufacturing analysis.
motivation: The brief was to design a device enabling individuals with limited mobility and dexterity to effectively remove garden weeds across different soil types. Market research showed 75+ year-olds are among the highest spenders on garden equipment, and that 54% of state-pension-age adults report mobility issues — making this a genuinely underserved user group rather than a generic gardening tool.
methodology: The team benchmarked four existing products, built a formal requirements list (performance, ergonomics, safety, force specs), and each member generated an individual concept — I designed the 'Adjustable Weed Grabber' concept, a spring-loaded, telescoping-shaft tool with an ergonomic rubber-grip handle. Concepts were scored in a weighted Pugh-style evaluation matrix, and the final hybrid design combined my telescoping shaft and grip handle with a multi-functional tool head and clip-on wheels from the other concepts. Materials were shortlisted using Ashby charts against density, strength, cost and recyclability, and injection moulding was selected over compression moulding after a cycle-time and tooling-cost comparison. A lifecycle eco-audit quantified energy and CO2e by phase.
results: The final design telescopes from 0.3m to 0.9m with magnetic-seal locking joints, a quick-release stainless-steel tool-attachment mechanism, a two-fork weed-gripping head plus an alternate foot-pedal deep-root tool, and optional clip-on wheels. The eco-audit found the material phase dominates lifecycle energy and CO2e, with manufacturing at ~22%/32% and recycling offsetting roughly 47%/39% of energy/CO2e respectively.
